claims.text: High configurational entropy helps high-entropy nanoalloys maintain a single-phase structure at high temperatures.
High configurational entropy impedes diffusion-driven segregation of constituent elements.
The nanoalloys begin in a homogeneous, disordered, single-phase state.
The proposed dopant is a low-diffusivity element in the relevant high-entropy nanoalloy.
Diffusion processes are activated during treatment at 600–800 °C.
An inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation during treatment at 600–800 °C.
Internal grain boundaries and interfacial regions in the disordered high-entropy state create increased barriers to atomic migration.
Disordered atomic configurations raise the activation energy for atomic diffusion.
Higher activation energy for diffusion suppresses the kinetics of chemical segregation.
Higher activation energy for diffusion suppresses phase decomposition.
Chemical segregation and phase decomposition would otherwise cause structural instability.
Low-diffusivity-element doping will reduce phase segregation relative to the undoped baseline after identical high-temperature exposure.
Low-diffusivity-element doping will improve retention of lattice parameters relative to the undoped baseline.
Low-diffusivity-element doping will improve retention of hardness relative to the undoped baseline.
The standard undoped high-entropy nanoalloy is expected to undergo moderate segregation during the thermal treatment.
The standard undoped high-entropy nanoalloy is expected to undergo phase decomposition during the thermal treatment.
The prediction applies where diffusion is the primary driver of instability under high-temperature inert conditions.
Behavior may differ at temperatures significantly above 900 °C.
Behavior may differ in oxidizing environments.
